news.title: 600,000 Card Numbers Stolen From Online Checkouts
news.excerpt: Thieves have been slipping a few lines of sneaky code onto the checkout pages of more than a hundred online shops, so every card number typed in gets quietly copied to them. Over 600,000 cards have been taken since July, according to security researchers. The shops look normal — you can't spot this scam by looking. Check your last card statement today and report anything you don't recognize. I've switched to a credit card for online shopping, never a debit card — it's far easier to get your money back.

news.title: ASUS Store Hack — Expect Fake Order Emails
news.excerpt: ASUS, the company that makes laptops and computer parts, says someone got into its online store and took customers' names, email addresses, phone numbers, and order records. No card numbers were taken. The danger now is fake messages that quote your real order to sound believable. If an email or a call asks you to confirm an ASUS order, don't click and don't call the number it gives you — open your browser and type asus.com yourself. I've seen these; they always rush you.

news.title: Weber Shut Off Its June Oven's App — Check Whether Your Own Smart Gadgets Still Work
news.excerpt: Last Tuesday, Weber switched off the servers behind its June countertop oven. People paid up to $1,500, and now the app, the camera, and the guided cooking are gone — the oven only bakes. Nothing broke; the company just turned it off. Any gadget in your house that runs on the maker's servers can be next. The two-minute check: open the app for each smart device you own. If it cannot work without signing in to the company's account, that gadget has an expiration date.

news.title: That Call About a Warrant Is a Scam — Real Police Never Demand Money
news.excerpt: If your phone rings and the caller says you missed jury duty, or that a judge signed a paper for your arrest, hang up — it's a scam. Callers fake the real number of your local sheriff's office, keep you on the line, and take payment in gift cards, wires or cash. Police never phone you to collect money. Hang up, then call the sheriff's office at a number you look up yourself.

news.title: Microsoft's September Patches May Have Quietly Stopped Your Backups
news.excerpt: Microsoft says the patches it sent out this month can quietly stop the tool that copies your files for you. On some computers the last-backup date freezes, Windows keeps asking you to reconnect a perfectly good drive, and older versions of your files disappear. No scam to spot here — nothing was stolen; the safety net just stopped working. Press Start, type File History, and check that date. If it's stale, copy your Documents, Pictures and Desktop onto a USB drive until Microsoft ships a fix.

posts.title: Is your computer running slow? Microsoft's free PC Manager tidies it up in one click — get it from the Microsoft Store or pcmanager.microsoft.com
posts.summary: Go to pcmanager.microsoft.com — or open the Microsoft Store, search Microsoft PC Manager, and install it. It is free, and it is made by Microsoft rather than by some outfit selling you a yearly plan. Open it and press the big Boost button. It sweeps out temporary junk files, shows you which apps open by themselves the moment you turn the computer on, and runs a quick health check in one tap. Works on Windows 10 and Windows 11.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize the thing making a computer feel tired is not its age. It is the pile-up. Every piece of software you ever installed adds a little helper that starts itself the second you sign in, and after two or three years there can be thirty of them all shoving toward the front door at once. The honest answer is that the machine is usually fine — it is just being asked to do too much at the same second. I see this all the time: somebody is about to pay 600 dollars for a new laptop at a big-box store when the real trouble is a five-minute tidy-up. Try the free tidy-up first. If it does not help, then we talk about new hardware, and you will know for sure instead of guessing.

posts.title: Is your computer still under factory warranty? Dell, HP and Lenovo look it up free from the serial number on the sticker
posts.summary: Turn the laptop over, or look at the back of a desktop tower, and find the white sticker with the serial number. On a Dell it is called the Service Tag — seven letters and numbers. Type it into the maker's own page: dell.com/support for Dell, support.hp.com for HP, and pcsupport.lenovo.com for Lenovo (look for warranty lookup there). It shows the exact date your coverage ends, in seconds, with no account to create. Write that date on a piece of tape and stick it to the bottom of the machine. It settles arguments later.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize they are sitting on coverage they already paid for. The honest answer is that a three-year-old machine can still have a year of factory warranty left, and the owner has no idea, because nobody ever told them. That sticker is the first thing I check in the shop: before I quote a price, I check whether the maker should be paying for the part instead of you. I see this all the time — somebody buys a used laptop at a yard sale or from a friend and never asks about the warranty, when in fact the leftover coverage traveled right along with the machine. Two minutes and that number tells you whether a fix is on you or on Dell.

posts.title: Google put Gemini on your Windows PC for free — install it from gemini.google/desktop and press Alt+Space to ask it anything
posts.summary: Go to gemini.google/desktop and download the free Gemini app for Windows (it runs on Windows 10 and 11). Then press Alt and Space together, and a small box opens right on top of whatever you are doing. Ask it to rewrite an email so it sounds kinder, explain a letter you got in the mail, put a long article into three sentences, or give you a recipe from what is already in your fridge. It is free with your Google account, and it stays out of the way until you call for it.
posts.truth: Most people think of AI as a website you go visit. The honest answer is that it is now about as hard as pressing two keys — and that changes how useful it is. The question I get every week is "should I be using it?" My answer: for words, yes, use it freely. It is very good at explaining a confusing letter, fixing the tone of an email to a grandchild, or telling you what a confusing error message means. What it should never see is your passwords, your Social Security number, or your bank login. I see this all the time: folks are either scared of it or they trust it with everything. The right place is in the middle.

posts.title: A file called photo.jpg.exe is not a photo — turn on "File name extensions" in Windows File Explorer to see a file's real name
posts.summary: Open any folder, click View at the top of the window, point to Show, and click File name extensions. Now every file shows its real ending. A file named photo.jpg is a picture; one named photo.jpg.exe is a program wearing a picture's name. Windows hides those endings by default, and that's exactly what scammers count on. It's free, it's already on every Windows PC, and it takes about ten seconds.
posts.truth: Most people think Windows hides file endings to keep things tidy. The honest answer is that hiding them is what makes the trick work. I see this all the time: someone opens what looks like a photo, a receipt, or an invoice from an email, double-clicks it, and instead of a picture, a program starts running. You don't need an antivirus to catch that one — you just need to see the real name before you click. Turn File name extensions on today — open any folder, click View at the top, point to Show, and you're done.

posts.title: Chrome will start warning you about old-style "not private" websites in October — turn on Always Use Secure Connections now in Chrome's Settings
posts.summary: Starting in October, Google Chrome will begin warning you before it opens an older-style website that doesn't have the little padlock. You can turn that protection on right now instead of waiting. Open Chrome, click the three dots at the top right, then Settings > Privacy and security > Security, and switch on Always use secure connections. It's free and takes under a minute.
posts.truth: Here's the part that surprises people: the padlock is not about whether a website is honest — it's about whether the connection is private. A fake page can have a padlock too. But when the padlock is missing, what you type and the passwords you enter can be read by someone in the middle, and that's how folks get burned on public Wi-Fi at coffee shops, laundromats, and hotels. Turning this on means Chrome taps you on the shoulder before it walks you onto the unlit side of the street. Do it once and it's done.

posts.title: Google just plugged 108 security holes in Chrome — update yours free in one minute at chrome://settings/help
posts.summary: Open Chrome, type chrome://settings/help into the address bar, and press Enter. Chrome looks for the newest version on its own, so you are not hunting for a download. If it says Chrome is up to date, you are done. If a newer version is waiting, it installs and shows you a Relaunch button — click it once and your browser reopens, already protected. Free, about a minute, and no account needed.
posts.truth: That little dot at the top right corner of the window is not decoration — it means a newer version is sitting there ready and not yet in use. The honest answer is that on a web browser, the distance between protected and exposed is often one click that nobody ever noticed. I see this all the time: a machine comes in and the browser has been months behind, and the owner did nothing wrong — they just never closed the window, because they always keep a dozen tabs open for the bank and the church and the grandkids. Google shipped 108 safeguards at once this week. That is a lot of doors being locked while yours waits on a restart you did not know you owed.

posts.title: Grandma's cassette tapes won't last forever — Audacity is the free app at audacityteam.org that records them onto your computer as MP3s
posts.summary: Go to audacityteam.org and download Audacity — it is free, open source, and runs on Windows and Mac. You will need a cord from the tape deck's headphone or line-out jack into your computer's microphone or line-in jack (a few dollars at Walmart or on Amazon). Open Audacity, press Record, press Play on the tape deck, and let the whole side run through. Then use File > Export to save it as an MP3 you can email, put on a flash drive, or burn to a CD. Nothing is uploaded anywhere — the whole thing happens on your own machine, with no account and no internet needed.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize a cassette tape has a shelf life. The tape stretches, the little felt pad inside falls off, the rubber belt in the player turns to goo, and the machines that play them stopped being made a long time ago. That wedding tape, the sermon, the grandkids singing at church in 1988 — the tape is the only copy and it is quietly dying in a closet. The honest answer is that the fix costs nothing but an afternoon and a five-dollar cable. And it is not just tapes: the same free program takes the sound off a record player or a VHS tape. I see this all the time — somebody brings in an old tape deck hoping the computer can read it. The computer can't read it, but it can most certainly listen to it.

posts.title: New laptops are about to cost 5% to 20% more — Windows' own Settings > System > About shows whether yours can go another year
posts.summary: Click Start, type about, and open About your PC — the same page as Settings > System > About. It names your processor and shows how much working space your apps have to run in. Write those two lines down on paper. Now here is the news: Acer's chief executive said this week that computer prices will climb another 5% to 20% by the end of 2026, because the parts inside have been getting more expensive all year. So before you spend on a new machine, let somebody look at the one you own. If it is healthy inside, a good going-over and a fresh setup can keep it running for years — and if you truly do need a new one, buying sooner is cheaper than buying in December.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize that the two lines on that About page are the whole story. The honest answer is that a computer which feels slow is usually not worn out — it is tripping over years of piled-up software, and no new laptop on the shelf magically avoids that. I see this all the time: somebody buys a new machine, moves everything over the way it was, and three months later it feels just as slow as the old one did. Meanwhile the old machine was a five-minute look away from being fine. Prices are climbing because the memory inside every computer got dramatically more expensive this year — that is real, and it is not coming back down soon. Which makes the old question worth asking first: does yours actually need leaving?

posts.title: That Amazon "deal" price may be higher than it was last month — CamelCamelCamel shows the real price history free at camelcamelcamel.com
posts.summary: Copy the web address of the Amazon item you're looking at, paste it into the search box at camelcamelcamel.com (yes, that's the real name), and you'll get a simple chart of what it actually cost over the past months — including the lowest price it has ever been. You can set a free alert, and it will email you when the price really drops. You don't need an account just to look up a price.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize a "sale" price is sometimes higher than the normal price was a few weeks earlier. That matters right now, with the holiday deal season about to start and gadget prices bouncing around all year. The honest answer is that the only way to know if a deal is real is to look at the history — and the history is free. Don't take the red tag's word for it.

posts.title: That shocking photo might be AI — Chrome's built-in "About this image" check tells you in one right-click, free and built in
posts.summary: If a picture in your feed looks too wild to be true, you can check it. In Chrome, right-click the photo and choose About this image. Google looks for a hidden, invisible mark called SynthID that it adds to pictures made with its AI tools, and it tells you what it finds. It's free and already built into Chrome — nothing to install.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize how good the fakes have gotten. A few years ago you could spot a fake photo by the extra fingers. Not anymore. The honest answer is that you can no longer trust your eyes alone, so stop and check before you believe a wild picture — and especially before you forward it. One thing to know: this check only catches pictures that were made by Google's AI tools. If it says no mark was found, that does not prove the photo is real. It just means Google didn't find its own watermark.
